blocks.text: Covalent bonds behave rather like springs and can vibrate in several ways: stretching (symmetric or asymmetric) and bending. The frequencies of these vibrations lie in the infrared region of the spectrum. When an organic molecule is irradiated with infrared energy that matches the natural vibration frequency of one of its bonds, it absorbs some of that energy and the amplitude of the vibration increases.

blocks.alt: Three sketches of a central blue atom with two yellow atoms: symmetric stretching (both outer atoms moving outward together), asymmetric stretching (one moving out as the other moves in) and bending (the angle opening and closing).
blocks.caption: Ways in which bonds vibrate (original sketch after Figure 29.6).
blocks.long_description: Each kind of vibration has its own frequency. Infrared radiation of exactly that frequency is absorbed, but only if the vibration changes the molecule's dipole moment.

blocks.text: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy identifies compounds from the changes in vibration when they absorb IR of specific frequencies. A spectrophotometer passes IR radiation through the sample and detects how much is absorbed. IR energy is absorbed only if the molecule has a dipole that changes as it vibrates, so symmetrical, non-polar molecules such as O2 and H2 are IR inactive. Polar bonds such as O-H and N-H absorb at higher wavenumbers, and so do shorter bonds and multiple bonds (such as the triple bond of ethyne), because these bonds are stronger and need more energy.

An IR spectrum has two regions: the fingerprint region below 1500 cm^-1 and the functional group region above 1500 cm^-1. Only the functional group region is used here, which is enough to identify the type of organic compound.

blocks.caption: IR absorption ranges of functional groups (book's Table 29.2)

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Infrared spectroscopy is used in some modern roadside breathalysers: an IR beam passes through the breath in the chamber, the characteristic bonds of ethanol are detected, and the more ethanol in the breath, the more IR is absorbed. IR sensors are also used to measure carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and unburnt hydrocarbons in vehicle emissions on motorways and in busy town centres.

blocks.prompt: Why are O2 and N2 not detected by IR spectroscopy, while CO2 is?
blocks.explanation: O2 and N2 have no dipole and their only vibration (stretching) does not create one, so they absorb no IR. CO2 has polar bonds; its asymmetric stretch and bending change the dipole, so it absorbs IR.

items: Bonds vibrate (stretch, bend); IR absorbed when the dipole changes.
Functional group region above 1500 cm-1; fingerprint region below.
